samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> According to a report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the contiguous U.S. experienced its 9th-warmest August in the 129-year climate record. The average temperature across the contiguous U.S. for August 2023 was 74.4 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 2.3 degrees above average. Several southern states reported their hottest August on record, including Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Texas experienced its second-hottest August. The meteorological summer, from June 1 to August 31, 2023, was the 15th-hottest on record for the contiguous U.S., with an average temperature of 73.0 degrees Fahrenheit, 1.6 degrees above average. Louisiana recorded its warmest summer on record, while Texas and Florida had their second-warmest. NASA also confirmed that the summer of 2023 was the hottest globally since records began in 1880. <2> A significant late-season heatwave impacted the Midwestern and Great Lakes regions of the United States in early September 2023. A strong heat dome led to temperatures 20-25°F above normal, with daily highs soaring into the 90s and even reaching 100°F in some areas, shattering long-standing records. The most intense period of heat occurred over Labor Day weekend, from approximately September 2nd to September 4th. [4, 6, 7] States particularly affected included Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, Illinois, and Michigan. [6, 7] In Minnesota, the Twin Cities recorded temperatures of 97°F and 98°F on September 3rd and 4th respectively. [6] Duluth, Minnesota, registered its first-ever temperature at or above 95°F in September, hitting 97°F on September 3rd. [6, 8] Wisconsin also experienced record or near-record heat, with Wausau and Eau Claire reaching 99°F and 100°F. [6] The heatwave was characterized as the most severe September heatwave on record east of the Rockies by at least one weather historian. [8] A second, less intense, period of record-breaking warmth, primarily characterized by unusually high minimum temperatures, was observed in the Upper Midwest from September 22nd to 30th. [5] <3> A severe heatwave gripped the U.S. during the summer of 2023, with a particularly intense period in late August affecting an estimated 130 million people across at least 19 states in the Midwest and Gulf regions. This extreme weather event, described as a large heat dome, brought record-breaking temperatures and led to a significant surge in electricity demand. The increased need for cooling placed considerable strain on the power grids managed by the Southwest Power Pool (SPP), Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT). These grid operators experienced substantial increases in electricity demand, with ERCOT setting an all-time peak demand record of over 85,500 megawatts on August 10, 2023. The heatwave also highlighted the challenges of renewable energy generation, as wind power output decreased during the peak, necessitating an increased reliance on natural gas and coal to maintain grid stability. <4> A significant heatwave, driven by a large 'heat dome,' impacted the U.S. Midwest and South in late August 2023, setting numerous temperature records. [9, 14, 15] On August 24, Chicago recorded a temperature of 100°F for the first time since July 2012, with the heat index at O'Hare Airport reaching as high as 120°F. [8, 20] That same day, Houston tied its all-time high temperature of 109°F, a record also met on August 27. [11, 16, 17] The heat was widespread, with heat index values of 120-125°F reported in parts of Iowa and Missouri. [15, 21] Specifically, Sioux City, Iowa, set a new all-time record heat index of 122°F on August 21, and Kansas City, Missouri, tied its all-time record of 120°F on August 20. [21] Hundreds of record-high and record-warm-low temperatures were anticipated across a region stretching from Minnesota to Louisiana. [9] <5> Phoenix, Arizona, experienced a record-breaking streak of 31 consecutive days with temperatures at or exceeding 110°F (43.3°C). The streak began on June 30, 2023, and concluded on July 30, 2023. [8] This event shattered the previous record of 18 straight days set in 1974. [6] The day the streak ended, July 31, 2023, the high temperature was a cooler 108°F. [3] This extended period of extreme heat was part of a broader sweltering summer for the city, which included the hottest July on record for Phoenix. [6, 8] <6> On July 27, 2023, the Biden-Harris administration directed the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) to issue the nation's first-ever Heat Hazard Alert. This alert reaffirms that workers have federal protections from extreme heat and reminds employers of their legal obligation to provide safe working conditions. In conjunction with the alert, the administration announced that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) would intensify its enforcement of heat safety violations. This includes increasing inspections in high-risk industries such as construction and agriculture. The move is part of a broader effort to protect workers and communities from the rising dangers of extreme heat, which is the leading cause of weather-related deaths in the United States. <7> In June 2023, a series of record-breaking heatwaves brought dangerous conditions to large portions of the United States. The heat was particularly intense in the Southeast, with some areas in Mississippi and Louisiana experiencing heat index values approaching 120°F. The Midwest also faced hazardous conditions, with 'feels-like' temperatures reaching between 100 and 115°F in late June. A National Weather Service office in Paducah, Kentucky, noted that the region was likely experiencing its warmest temperatures since 2012. These heatwaves were part of a broader pattern of extreme weather that month, which also included significant smoke from Canadian wildfires affecting air quality in the Northeast and Great Lakes regions. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) confirmed that June 2023 was marked by these record-setting heatwaves and other severe weather events across the country. <8> A retrospective report by NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information confirmed that multiple heatwaves brought record-setting temperatures to various parts of the U.S. during June 2023. [1, 2, 3] Significant heat events impacted Puerto Rico, the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic, Great Lakes, and the southern Plains, including Texas and Louisiana. [1, 2] Specific records noted in the report include a daily temperature of 95 degrees F in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on June 6, and a temperature of 119 degrees F in Rio Grande Village, Texas, on June 24. [1] <9> A severe and deadly heatwave struck Texas throughout June 2023, causing record-breaking temperatures, a surge in heat-related illnesses, and numerous fatalities. The intense heat, which saw temperatures climb to 119 degrees Fahrenheit in Rio Grande Village on June 24th, placed significant strain on the state's power grid. The heatwave's severity was underscored by a dramatic increase in emergency room visits for heat-related issues, with at least 350 visits on June 20th alone. Tragically, the extreme conditions were linked to at least a dozen deaths across the region. The persistent high temperatures, with some areas experiencing consecutive days over 100 degrees, also led to concerns about the stability of the power supply, though widespread outages were avoided, partly due to the significant contribution of solar power. The event prompted public health warnings and the opening of cooling centers in many cities to provide relief to residents. <10> In early June 2023, Puerto Rico endured a prolonged and historic heatwave, which was part of a broader Caribbean heat event. The heat index reached an extreme 125 degrees Fahrenheit (52°C) in northern parts of the island, creating life-threatening conditions. On June 6, 2023, the capital, San Juan, recorded a new daily high temperature of 95 degrees Fahrenheit. Scientists attributed the intense heat to a confluence of factors: a high-pressure system, dust from the Sahara, high humidity, and record-breaking Atlantic Ocean temperatures likely intensified by human-caused climate change. The severe conditions led to significant societal impacts, including widespread health concerns and major power outages that affected over 100,000 customers due to a power plant failure during a period of high demand.

Subsequently, on October 10, 2025, hundreds of federal workers were laid off across the Department of Health and Human Services. These layoffs notably affected the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, which could negatively impact future heat response capabilities, especially since most heat-related activities are not statutorily authorized, potentially leading to more cuts. <2> On October 3, 2025, a rare and powerful October heat dome was reported to be forming across the U.S. farm belt, posing a significant threat to the agricultural sector. Forecasts indicated that temperatures could surpass 90°F in 24 states, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) assigning a high probability of above-normal heat between October 8 and 12. This unseasonal heat jeopardized late-season corn and soybean yields by potentially disrupting the harvest and accelerating crop drying. The heat also created stressful conditions for livestock, increasing the risk of reduced feed intake, slower weight gain, and higher mortality for animals such as poultry and cattle. <3> A significant fall heatwave brought summer-like temperatures to the central United States in early October 2025, with temperatures soaring 20 to 30 degrees above normal across the Midwest and northern Plains. Forecasts issued as early as September 30th anticipated highs in the upper 80s and low 90s for several states, including Minnesota, South Dakota, and Illinois. The heatwave resulted in record-breaking temperatures, as predicted. On Saturday, October 4, 2025, Minneapolis-St. Paul set a new daily record high of 91°F, making it the second-hottest October day in the area's recorded history. That same day also tied the record for the warmest overnight low at 72°F. The unusual warmth, which affected cities from Omaha to Chicago, was attributed to a strong ridge of high pressure stalled over the region. <4> Scientists have attributed record-breaking warm fall temperatures across many parts of the United States and Canada in the autumn of 2025 to a massive marine heat wave in the northern Pacific Ocean. This phenomenon, known as the "warm blob," was the fourth-largest on record and at one point in September covered nearly 3 million square miles, an area roughly the size of the contiguous U.S. The expansive and record-breaking ocean heat altered the jet stream, causing it to meander farther north than usual. This shift allowed summer-like heat to persist into October, with temperatures in some areas soaring 20 to 30 degrees above average. In the 30 days leading up to mid-October, over 1,800 record high temperatures were set in the U.S. While the heat wave drove unseasonable warmth in the fall, some scientists suggest it could also lead to a colder, snowier winter in the Midwest and eastern U.S. by causing a significant dip in the jet stream. <5> An intense heat dome brought record-breaking, summer-like temperatures to the Pacific Northwest and southwestern Canada in early September 2025. A blocked weather pattern, described as an omega block, caused temperatures to rise 20 to 30 degrees above normal for that time of year. On September 3rd, Ashcroft, British Columbia set a new Canadian record for the highest temperature in September at 40.8°C (105.4°F). Experts noted that states like Connecticut, which are experiencing hotter summers due to climate change, often do not have well-established summer shelter systems, unlike the more common cold-weather protocols. This lack of infrastructure increases the vulnerability of unhoused individuals, who are disproportionately affected by heat-related health risks. <7> A severe heatwave in the Western U.S. in late August 2025 created critical fire weather conditions, placing more than 30 million people under extreme weather alerts by Sunday, August 24, 2025. The fatalities, including at least three workers who died in late June 2025 during a widespread “heat dome,” coincided with OSHA public hearings on the proposed rule, which were held from June 16 to July 2, 2025. The proposal under discussion would mandate that employers provide workers with access to water, rest, and shade. A final version of the rule is anticipated by late 2025 or early 2026, to be followed by a phase-in period for employers. <9> Boston Mayor Michelle Wu declared a three-day heat emergency for the city, effective from Monday, August 11, 2025, through Wednesday, August 13, 2025. [4, 9] The declaration was made in response to forecasts predicting the heat index would reach between 95 and 96 degrees. [4] To help residents cope with the extreme heat, the city opened cooling centers at all Boston Centers for Youth & Families (BCYF) locations during their normal operating hours. [4, 11] Additionally, Boston Public Library branches were available as places for residents to find relief from the heat. [5, 11] Mayor Wu urged community members to stay safe, check on their neighbors, and stay cool during the period of intense heat. [5] <10> On August 8, 2025, the National Centers for Environmental Information reported that the Climate Prediction Center's forecast for August indicated a high probability of above-average temperatures for large portions of the United States. The highest chances for warmer-than-average conditions were noted for the Southwest, central Rockies, the Florida Peninsula, and the far Northeast, with above-average temperatures also favored across much of the West and East. This forecast followed a period of significant heat in the preceding months of 2025. For the contiguous U.S., July 2025's average temperature was 75.4°F, which is 1.8°F above the 20th-century average, placing it in the warmest third of the 131-year historical record. Several states experienced notable warmth, with Virginia and West Virginia tying their warmest July on record, and 12 states recording their warmest average minimum temperatures. For the year-to-date (January through July), the contiguous U.S. temperature was 2.0°F above average, also ranking in the warmest third of the historical record.
